newsitem.title: USA: US rail freight traffic up from year ago--AAR.
newsitem.headline: US rail freight traffic up from year ago--AAR.

text.p: U.S. rail freight traffic as measured in carloads and intermodal rose in the week ended October 5 from the same week a year ago, the Association of American Railroads said Thursday.

AAR said carloads, at 358,914 in the week, were up 3.2 percent from 347,724 a year ago. Intermodal traffic, which does not include carloads, rose 5.3 percent to 174,591 trailers and containers from 165,758 in the year-ago week.
AAR said ton-miles also climbed 3.9 percent to 26.6 billion from 25.6 billion last year. A ton mile is equal to one ton of freight hauled one mile.
"This week can be summed up in three words: grain, coal and intermodal," Harvey Levine, AAR chief economist, said.
"Grain loadings continue very weak, but strong loadings of coal and intermodal were able to give the week an overall increase from last year," Levine added.
Grain loadings fell 31.9 percent to 18,117 carloads from 26,592 last year, while coal carloads rose 9.2 percent to 143,880 from 131,748.

Other notable increases were in metals and related products, which rose 15 percent over a year ago, lumber and wood products which were up 6.7 percent, and petroleum, up 6.6 percent. Nonmetallic minerals also rose 6.8 percent, AAR said.
Farm products other than grain, metallic ores and primary forest products posted declines from the year-ago week.
In the first 40 weeks of 1996, AAR said ton-miles rose 1.9 percent from the same period last year. Intermodal traffic also rose 1.1 percent, but carloads fell 0.8 percent, AAR said.
